areas.title: Labor markets
areas.q: What do public data say about each occupation, below the official figures?
areas.overview: At Radius I kept being asked about particular occupations: how many people leave them, where their workers come from, what training into them leads to. The official statistics could answer only for broad groups, so I started building the answers myself from public data, the same way for every detailed occupation and, where I could, every state. Each paper below is one of those estimates, checked against the official figures and put to work on a question someone actually asked me. The research and the writing are my own, not Radius’s.

areas.title: AI and work
areas.q: What is AI doing to the work employers ask for?
areas.overview: Every question I was asked about AI and jobs came with an exposure index that ranks jobs without saying what it measures. Writing the labor market as one wage bill at three levels, occupations, tasks and skills, shows what each measure can identify and lets me follow AI into what employers ask for. The next step is the activities AI could do but has not yet entered, and the measures feed AI at Work, a public index that updates with each data release.

areas.title: Regional development
areas.q: Why do Europe’s lagging regions stay behind?
areas.overview: I wanted to understand why Europe’s lagging regions stay behind after thirty years of cohesion funding. My PhD treats a region as an ecosystem of place, people and economy inside its national system, tests that view across the euro crisis and the pandemic, and fits a model of its dynamics to 210 regions. The next steps are causal designs for the links between the three domains and a network between regions beside the one within them.

areas.title: Macroeconomics
areas.q: UK tax policy, and wellbeing inside a macroeconomic model.
areas.overview: UK fiscal policy needed a better dating of tax shocks, because most tax changes are now announced months before they take effect. Dating them properly let me show that the same tax rise costs roughly twice as much in consumption when the economy has slack. Beside it, the wellbeing model from my master’s thesis, which puts a household’s social life inside macroeconomics, is being extended to France and to Europe’s regions.

areas.title: Data science
areas.q: Tools for reading occupations and the economy from text.
areas.overview: Most labor data starts as messy text, in job titles, job ads and reports, and I needed reliable ways to turn it into occupations and signals. These notes cover autocoding titles to the federal taxonomy, a taxonomy of roles finer than the federal codes, and labor sentiment read from the Federal Reserve’s Beige Book. Each could grow into a public tool.

nodes.title: An occupational flow account for the United States, 2009 to 2025
nodes.date: Begun 2025 · in progress, replaces the 2025 working paper
nodes.plain: How often do people really change occupation? The standard survey is a shaky guide, as a growing share of its answers are filled in from other people. I rebuild the count on the people who actually answered, for every occupation, along with where its workers come from and where they go.

nodes.title: Distance and occupation in interstate migration: a gravity measure for 209 occupations
nodes.date: Begun 2025 · in progress, replaces the 2026 working paper
nodes.plain: How far does an employer have to look for a welder, a nurse or a software developer? I measure how quickly interstate moves into each occupation fall off with distance, and use it to show where out-of-state hires are likely to come from.

nodes.title: Realized exits from the labor force by detailed occupation
nodes.plain: Workforce plans assume how many people will leave an occupation each year, usually with a rate modeled on broad groups. From the monthly labor force survey, I measure the realized rate and the reasons for leaving for each detailed occupation.

nodes.title: Outcomes after publicly funded training: new measures from public WIOA records
nodes.plain: Public training statistics say whether trainees find work, but not what kind. From the public records of the federal training program, I measure whether trainees end up in the field they trained for, how good their jobs are, and how outcomes differ by the occupation trained for.

nodes.title: Real pay by occupation across the United States
nodes.plain: A salary goes further in some states than in others. I combine pay for every occupation with state prices, weighted by what workers’ households actually spend, to show where each job pays best once the cost of living is counted.

nodes.title: AI exposure at three levels
nodes.date: Begun 2025 · working paper, May 2026, revised September 2026
nodes.plain: A labor market can be described three ways at once: by what each occupation is paid, by the tasks each occupation performs, and by the skills those tasks use. The three descriptions have to add up to the same wage bill, but they cannot all be tested the same way. Wages are observed once per occupation, so a description with more tasks than occupations will always fit the data, while one with fewer skills than occupations can be rejected. Each research team that has scored AI exposure scored one of these three levels. This paper places each score at the level where it was collected, and finds that the capability measures are one measure under three names. It then tests realized wages and employment through 2025. No skill group has shifted beyond its normal year-to-year variation, and every break in the series comes with the pandemic, two years before generative AI. So far generative AI has not shown up in the number of jobs or in what they pay, and the paper sets out the test on job postings that should pick it up first.
nodes.abs: Measures of exposure to generative artificial intelligence are collected at three levels of the labor market, occupations, tasks, and skills, and compared as though they described one object. This paper writes the labor market as one wage bill at three levels and counts what each can identify: 829 observed wages against an identity, against 17,383 task prices that no wage data can contradict, and against 25 skill prices that can. Which quantities in this literature are testable therefore follows from how many statements the analysts of the Occupational Information Network wrote at each level. The leading capability measures are, on inspection, one construct under three names. Converting the Eloundou task ratings to abilities reproduces the Felten ability scores in the right order across AI applications, the Srinivasan automation score is the Eloundou construction re-run on a later release, and a quadratic in automation explains 77 percent of augmentation. The skill layer supports a structure of about twenty-five dimensions, which explains occupational wages at a cross-validated 0.648 in the Network’s own named groups, and whose loadings are informative as changes over time but uninformative as levels. On a balanced panel of 693 occupations from 2012 to 2025, nothing in realized wages or employment has moved beyond ordinary volatility since language models were released. No skill group moved by more than 1.51 times its own year-to-year variation, and every deviation from the pre-2020 path begins with the pandemic. If the technology is changing what employers want, the change should appear in job postings before it appears in employment, and the paper specifies that test on the task composition of postings.
math: Y = Σₒ Eₒ wₒ, the wage bill as an identity over 829 occupations
wₒ = Σᵢ βₒᵢ pᵢ, an occupation’s wage as task shares times 17,383 task prices, never identified
pᵢ = Σₖ γᵢₖ πₖ, a task’s price as skill content times 25 skill prices, which can fail

nodes.title: Measurement limits: what standard task data can identify
nodes.plain: Most research on AI and work rests on the task data of the Occupational Information Network. This paper asks which quantities those data can support: which can be contradicted by wages and which cannot, and where conventional inference reports change that is not there.

nodes.title: What employers ask for
nodes.plain: Is AI changing what employers ask for, and does that change lead pay and jobs? A change in demand should appear in job ads before it appears in employment. This paper judges the content of ads against what ordinary years look like, separates exposure to AI from the business cycle and from the wider contraction in technology hiring, and tests whether ad content predicts pay and employment beyond ad volume.

nodes.title: Activities at risk
nodes.plain: Where could AI enter work but has not yet? This paper works at the level of activities rather than jobs or skills, maps the activities AI could do against those the usage data show it doing, and values the difference in wages. Its predictions about where AI enters next are registered before the data that test them arrive.

nodes.title: Does the choice of AI-exposure measure matter?
nodes.date: Begun 2025 · research note, June 2026, revised September 2026
nodes.plain: At least six serious measures score how exposed each occupation is to AI, and studies that report a share of jobs at risk usually pick one without saying why. If the measures disagree, any ranking of at-risk occupations reflects the choice of measure as well as the labor market. The usual comparison is a rank correlation, which weights an occupation of five hundred people the same as one of three million and is driven by the extremes, where all the measures agree. This note specifies a comparison of the measures by the wage dollars they classify as exposed, at a common cutoff and decile by decile, holding everything else fixed, and states in advance what each result would mean.
nodes.abs: At least six serious measures score how exposed each occupation is to artificial intelligence, and a study that reports the share of jobs at risk picks one of them, usually without saying why. If the measures agree, the choice is harmless. If they disagree, then every ranking of at-risk occupations, every regional exposure map, and every policy brief built on one of them reflects the instrument as well as the labor market, and no reader can tell by how much. This note specifies the comparison that policy needs and fixes its statistic. Rank correlations, the usual comparison, weight an occupation of five hundred people and one of three million equally, and they are dominated by the tails, where every measure agrees that telemarketers are exposed and roofers are not. Policy questions are posed on people and on dollars, and they are posed in the middle of the distribution, where the marginal occupation is classified one way or the other. The statistic is therefore the share of the wage bill on which two measures disagree about whether an occupation is exposed, at a common cut, together with the agreement rate by decile of the pooled ranking, which separates the extremes from the interior. The design holds population, occupational base, vintage, and every downstream computation fixed and varies only the measure, which is possible because the model built alongside the companion paper takes each measure as an interchangeable input. The readings that decide whether the choice matters are written down before the numbers are.
math: Dₐᵦ(q) = Σₒ ωₒ |1[o ∈ Xₐ(q)] − 1[o ∈ Xᵦ(q)]|, the share of the wage bill one measure calls exposed and the other does not

nodes.title: Skill prices after the release
nodes.plain: If generative AI had changed what skills earn or who is employed by 2025, the official occupational wage and employment statistics should show it. A recent task-based projection expects the returns to social and manual skills to rise and the return to analytical skills to fall. This note tests that projection on realized wages and employment from 2012 to 2025, with the skill groups fixed before any outcome was examined.

nodes.title: Silent AI
nodes.plain: From 2022 the vendors of software many jobs already use began to build generative AI into it, so a job ad that asks for a spreadsheet program can read the same in 2021 and in 2025 while the program it asks for now carries AI. This note asks whether occupations whose software gained AI in this silent way afterwards begin to ask for AI explicitly in their ads. The test was registered before it was run.

nodes.title: The O*NET technology record
nodes.plain: O*NET’s technology lists are the main official record of the software each occupation uses. If AI software has entered work since 2022, this record is one place it could appear. This note describes how far it has, release by release.

nodes.title: A regional development ecosystem framework: place, people and economy in European regions and their national systems
nodes.plain: About 1.5 trillion euros of European cohesion funding has been spent since 1989, and the map of lagging regions looks much as it did. The gap between what aggregate indicators report and what people in those regions experience has also grown. People working in community organizations, community colleges and workforce boards already treat a region’s places, people and economy as connected, because in their daily work they are, but the research behind their funding mostly studies one pair at a time. This paper assembles those pairwise findings into one system of three pillars, names the six pathways between them, and derives five propositions about how a region should behave in calm years and under a shock, which the next two papers test and then fit.
nodes.abs: In this paper I propose a framework for understanding regional economic development as an ecosystem, in which three domains, Place-based Conditions, Human and Social Capital and Economic Activity, act on one another and do not add up as separate factors. European regional disparities have persisted despite roughly 1.5 trillion euro of cohesion funding since 1989. A gap has also grown between what aggregate indicators report and what people in those regions experience. My premise is that neither is well explained by approaches that treat infrastructure, human capital and economic performance one at a time. A substantial literature already establishes that these domains interact, one pair at a time, and several measurement traditions already score regions on many dimensions side by side. However, neither models the system as a whole. The framework draws these strands together by naming the enabling, mediating and feedback mechanisms that run between the three pillars and giving each its precedent in the literature, and from them I derive five propositions about how regions should behave in calm conditions and under a shock, which the empirical companion tests on European NUTS 2 data. The framework is presented as a dynamic system, in which regions settle into stable but shiftable configurations. Its unit is the region inside its national system, since the level a region settles at is set largely by its country, and the regional part is the balance between the pillars and the speed at which an imbalance is corrected. In the companion, the euro crisis, which entered through the economy, pulled the economic pillar away from the social and territorial ones, which is the pattern the framework implies. The pandemic, by contrast, arrived through a different channel and did not separate them. This paper is the first of a sequence. It is followed by the empirical test and by a linear state-space model of the ecosystem, fitted to an annual panel of European regions from 2000 to 2023 in the form ecologists use to estimate a community matrix from time series.

nodes.title: Two crises, one structure: coupling and scale in European regional ecosystems
nodes.plain: If a region’s development were a single quantity, its parts would always move together. In calm years they almost do, and one factor fits thirty-five regional indicators better than three. The two shocks in the panel then behave differently. The euro crisis, which entered through the economy, pulled the Mediterranean economy away from its people and places and left it displaced a decade later, while the pandemic moved no bloc by much. Most of the gradient between regions is a gradient between countries, and within countries anti-establishment voting follows a region’s income level more than how long it has been stuck.
nodes.abs: In this paper I test the ecosystem framework of the conceptual companion, which organises regional development around three interacting pillars: Place-based Conditions, Human and Social Capital and Economic Activity. I use a cross-section of thirty-five indicators for 294 NUTS 2 regions in 2017 to 2019 and an annual panel of 152 regions in 23 countries from 2008 to 2023. Development is strongly organised in space, a single general factor fits the indicators better than three, and regions sort into four stable tiers, with between two thirds and nine tenths of the gradient lying between countries. The two shocks in the panel behave differently. Between 2008 and 2013 Mediterranean regions fell 0.52 standard deviations in relative position, with the economic pillar taking almost all of the fall and still displaced a decade later, whereas in the pandemic years no bloc moved by more than 0.18 and the South gained. The regions worst hit in one episode were no more likely than chance to be worst hit in the other. The correlation between the people and economy composites has declined since 2011, a slide that began with the recovery from the euro crisis. A development-trap index built to the standard specification agrees with the two-shock account by bloc but bears no relation to the tiers. Within countries anti-establishment voting follows a region's level, chiefly its income, at the last election and more weakly at the one before, and bears no relation to its years in the trap, with both measured before each vote. A partial-correlation network over the indicators shows that, in this panel, most of the association behind the pairwise relations reported in the literature lies on one shared development dimension. The analysis is descriptive, and mechanisms are left to the modelling companion.

nodes.title: Slow ecosystems: regional development, national systems and the limits of cohesion policy in Europe, 2000 to 2023
nodes.plain: The third paper estimates the dynamics the first two could only describe, fitting a model of the three domains to 210 regions over 24 years in the form ecologists use to estimate a community matrix. Everywhere the system has one slow mode and two fast ones. The slow mode is a region’s level, set mostly by its country, and less than half of a gap in level closes within a working life. Imbalances between the domains are corrected within a generation, faster where countries spend more on education and on people of working age. Cohesion money spread thinly, in seven-year cycles, to the regions least able to absorb it, could not have moved the regions it exists for, and the paper sets out what a policy fitting the system would look like.
nodes.abs: Europe's regions have not converged in thirty years of cohesion policy, and the regions left behind are now where anti-system parties do best. Treating a region as an ecosystem of place, people and economy, I estimate its dynamics on 210 regions in 23 countries from 2000 to 2023 and test cohesion policy against them. Everywhere the system has one slow mode and two fast ones. The slow mode is a region's level, set mostly by the country, with a half-life of fifty-five to seventy years, and a century of regional income data agrees that less than half of a gap in level closes within a working life. The fast modes, imbalances between domains, are corrected within a generation. People lead the economy in the South, the economy leads people in the East, and in struggling regions the economy does not feed people at all. An economy hit alone, as in the euro crisis, keeps 52 per cent of its loss after twenty-five years in the South against 32 per cent in the East. Under maintained conditions about a seventh of regions stay in Europe's bottom quarter, seven of them under every assumption tried. Cohesion money, spread at an intensity that buys no relative gain, to regions that on the causal evidence absorb it least, in cycles far shorter than the decades the system takes to respond, could not have moved them. A policy fitting the system would be concentrated, sustained beyond a cycle and aimed at capacity where the economy cannot yet take the money.

nodes.title: The anticipation content of fiscal policy: UK tax measures, 1945–2019
nodes.plain: A tax change is announced on one date and takes effect on another. In Britain, the share of tax changes announced more than four months ahead has roughly quadrupled since the postwar decades, so most of them have been public for months by the time they take effect. The standard way of measuring the effect of tax policy treats a change as news on the day it takes effect. That was a fair approximation when most changes arrived that way, and it no longer is. The gap also follows a pattern. It depends on which tax is changed, where the Budget falls in the calendar, and to a lesser degree on whether an election is coming. Tax rises are about four times more likely than cuts to take effect after an election.
nodes.abs: Narrative tax shocks are dated by implementation, and the resulting series are pooled across decades. Using 2,252 UK tax measures announced between 1945 and 2019, I show that the interval between announcement and implementation has changed enough for such a series to mix two economically different objects. The share of the tax impulse announced more than 120 days before taking effect rises from 0.18 in 1945–79 to 0.70 since 2000, and the unanticipated component of the quarterly impulse falls roughly fivefold. Computing the same quantity from the century-long dataset of Cloyne et al. (2025), on their coding and their threshold, reproduces the series and extends it back to 0.02 in 1920–44. Its length is also systematic. Within the same Budget, National Insurance changes are 39 percentage points more likely than excise duties to arrive with long notice, the fiscal-year calendar produces long notice only when the Budget falls late in the year, and tax rises are four times more likely than cuts to take effect after an election. The rise dates to the early 1990s, when the Budget process was reformed in the name of scrutiny and predictability, and its macroeconomic consequences were never assessed; the crises of the period do not appear to have shortened it.

nodes.title: When to raise taxes: state dependence in the UK tax multiplier
nodes.plain: Governments choose when to raise taxes, but the research they rely on mostly reports one average number for the effect of a tax change. Using a century of UK narrative tax measures and quarterly household consumption from 1955, the paper finds that the same unanticipated tax rise costs about twice as much when the economy has slack. Consumption falls 7.3 percent at its trough, against 3.2 percent when there is no slack, and the difference is estimated directly with its own standard error. The paper uses consumption as the outcome because it responds more than output, and because the output result depends on a single 1979 Budget whose coded value changed fourfold between two versions of the same dataset. The aggregate data cannot yet show whose spending falls, and the paper names the household data that could.
nodes.abs: Using UK narrative tax measures from 1918 to 2018 and quarterly household consumption from 1955, I estimate the response of consumption to tax changes that were not anticipated, and split it by whether unemployment was above or below its own recent average when the change took effect. Against a tax rise worth one percent of annual GDP, consumption falls by 7.3 percent at its trough when there is slack and by 3.2 percent when there is not, so the same rise costs roughly twice as much in a slack economy. The difference is estimated directly, with its own standard error, and is significant at eight of seventeen horizons. Consumption is also the better outcome to study: it responds more than output, on three times as many horizons, and unlike the output response it survives the removal of the single Budget on which the published UK multiplier depends. The shock series reproduces Cloyne (2013) exactly before it is extended, which settles the dating conventions the estimate relies on. The aggregate record is too thin to separate one tax from another or to detect whether pre-announcement weakens the effect, and whose spending falls is a question for household data, which the paper identifies.

nodes.title: Wellbeing and macroeconomics: a SAGE approach
nodes.plain: Standard macroeconomic models give a household two choices, consume or rest, and little else it can want. That is part of why they keep being surprised by how people behave in a crisis. In this model a household manages its means and its needs within an economy, a set of social relationships and a physical place, so the support people draw on when a shock hits is part of the model. That changes how a household responds to a shock and what counts as recovering from it. A recovery that restores income but leaves the household’s social ties damaged no longer counts as a full recovery.
nodes.abs: The aim of this project is to develop an economic model that improves on existing ones in capturing wellbeing outcomes stemming from economic shocks. The premise is that personal welfare depends on more than just preference satisfaction and that the other determinants, which are affected by economic choices may not be captured by standard models. A theoretical approach for representing wellbeing more completely, the SAGE framework, is presented as the basis for this analysis and adapted to a Bewley-class model. Some parameters are derived from data while others are calibrated in an equilibrium state, and then a modest productivity shock is simulated to understand how groups in different wealth categories respond and what the wellbeing implications are. While the model needs further development, the results follow some general patterns observed in economic data and offer insights into behavior of the different wealth groups, including a decoupling of personal welfare dimensions following a productivity shock. In general, the introduction of wellbeing into the model shows promise for future development that better encompasses the motivations of groups and their responses to changes in their economic environments.

nodes.title: Wellbeing and macroeconomics notebook
nodes.plain: The paper argues that a household’s social life belongs inside the model. The notebook lets anyone test that claim by turning the social terms up and down and seeing which results change. The parameters it exposes are the ones the paper’s argument depends on.

nodes.title: Wellbeing and the social fabric in a heterogeneous-agent economy
nodes.plain: The SAGE paper put a household’s social life inside a macroeconomic model. This paper disciplines that model with French data and asks what economic policy does to the social side of wellbeing as well as the material side, and whether policy can pull the two apart.

nodes.title: Participation gradients and coordination traps: agency, social cohesion and activation policy
nodes.plain: Are left-behind communities caught in coordination traps, where people stay out of economic and civic life because others do? This paper asks what the observed differences in participation between groups can tell us about whether such traps exist at all.

nodes.title: Regional basins and the social fabric: fragility, national regimes and development
nodes.plain: Why do some regions stay fragile while others recover, and how much of that is set by the national regime they sit in? This paper takes the SAGE model to regions, where it meets the regional ecosystem work of the PhD.

nodes.title: Roles not titles: a role taxonomy anchored to the federal occupation system
nodes.plain: Federal occupation codes are too coarse for employers and job titles are too noisy. This note asks whether a finer taxonomy of roles can be built that nests strictly inside the federal codes, including the residual “All other” categories that hold so many workers.

nodes.title: Classification beats retrieval: the ceiling for occupational autocoding
nodes.plain: Assigning a detailed occupation code to a job title or a job ad is the first step in most labor-market work with text. This note asks how accurately it can be done at the eight-digit level, and whether a trained classifier or a retrieval approach gets closer to the ceiling.

nodes.title: Reading the Beige Book with LLMs
nodes.plain: Eight times a year the twelve Federal Reserve districts publish qualitative reports full of labor market detail, collected because the hard statistics arrive too late to be useful. Economists have mined them with dictionaries and hand-coding for decades. An LLM can pull structured labor sentiment out of each release for about thirteen cents, so the full forty-year archive costs a few hundred dollars to process. Once the archive is on the same district-by-quarter basis as the official series, it can be tested against them.
nodes.abs: The Federal Reserve Beige Book carries district-level qualitative labor-market reporting eight times a year, collected because hard statistics arrive with a lag, and it has historically been analyzed with keyword dictionaries or hand-coding. This note applies structured LLM extraction across the full forty-year archive at roughly thirteen cents per release, producing labor-market sentiment on the same district-by-quarter grain as the official series, with every extracted signal carrying the sentence it came from. The evaluation tests whether the extracted series carries information beyond the hard series it should lead, with the test specified before the extraction is scored. The resulting dataset is released publicly.
